paper_metadata.title: Quality of life and psychological health after mild traumatic brain injury in older people: Three- and six-month follow up

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the target population (older adults 65+), recruitment setting (The Alfred Trauma Centre), and explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria. The use of both trauma and community comparison groups strengthens the representativeness of the findings.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: All participants were aged ≥65 years and were fluent in English. Participants were also functionally independent (prior to injury) and resided within three hours of The Alfred Hospital, Melbourne Australia.
items.reasoning: The authors clearly define the age, language, functional status, and geographic location of the target population.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Consecutive trauma patients who presented to The Alfred Emergency & Trauma Centre between January 2016 and March 2019 were screened for eligibility using accessible medical records.
items.reasoning: The use of consecutive sampling from a major trauma center helps minimize selection bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between January 2016 and March 2019
items.reasoning: The specific dates for recruitment are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: The Alfred Trauma Centre in Melbourne, Australia
items.reasoning: The specific hospital and city are identified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients with mild TBI were identified using current criteria, which defines mTBI as blunt head trauma resulting in one or more of the following symptoms: (i) disorientation, (ii) loss of consciousness (LOC) ≤30 minutes, (iii) post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) ≤24 hours... Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score between 13 and 15
items.reasoning: The study uses standardized, internationally recognized clinical criteria for mTBI and lists specific health-related exclusions.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: One-hundred and 42 trauma patients agreed to participate in the study... Fifteen participants later withdrew, leaving a total of 106 trauma patients for analysis.
items.reasoning: The flow of participants is described, and the retention rate (106/142 = 74.6% of those who agreed) is reasonable for a longitudinal study, though slightly below the 80% ideal.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The three groups (i.e., mTBI, TC and CC) did not significantly differ on gender, age, years of education, or number of comorbidities (Table 1).
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides a comprehensive breakdown of demographics and injury characteristics across all three groups.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study accounts for missing data using multiple imputation and confirms that data were missing at random. The reasons for exclusion and withdrawal are documented.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: resulting in 8% of the total dataset being imputed.
items.reasoning: Only 8% of the data required imputation, suggesting a high rate of completion for the analyzed sample.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text mentions withdrawals but does not describe specific attempts to follow up with those who left the study.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Fifteen participants later withdrew
items.reasoning: The number of withdrawals is provided, but the specific reasons for withdrawal (e.g., health decline, loss of interest) are not detailed.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no comparison provided between the characteristics of those who completed the study and those who withdrew.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Little MCAR's analysis demonstrated that the data were missing at random, χ2 = 9770.867, df = 49695, p = 1.000
items.reasoning: While the MCAR test suggests no systematic bias in missingness, the lack of a direct comparison table for dropouts makes this difficult to verify definitively.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (GCS, neuroimaging, neuropsychological performance) were measured using standardized clinical tools and validated neuropsychological batteries. The methods were consistent across the mTBI group.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: GCS (dichotomized as GCS = 15 or GCS < 15), presence of abnormal neuroimaging, and 3-month neuropsychological performance
items.reasoning: The prognostic factors are clearly defined and operationalized for the regression model.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: These included the Hopkins Verbal Learning Test, Trail Making Test, Colour-Word Interference Task, and WAIS-IV Coding subtest
items.reasoning: The study uses gold-standard, validated neuropsychological tests.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: GCS (dichotomized as GCS = 15 or GCS < 15)
items.reasoning: The GCS cut-point is a standard clinical threshold for 'complicated' vs 'uncomplicated' mTBI.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Assessment and questionnaires were completed at 3 and 6 months after injury for the trauma groups
items.reasoning: The protocol was standardized for the clinical groups.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: resulting in 8% of the total dataset being imputed.
items.reasoning: The vast majority of PF data was available.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: conducted multiple imputation analysis that used proxies (i.e., similar variables across timepoints) to predict and replace the missing data
items.reasoning: Multiple imputation is an appropriate method for handling data missing at random.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The primary outcome (QoL) was measured using the WHOQOL-BREF, a globally validated instrument. The secondary outcome (Psychological Health) used the DASS-21, also highly validated. Measurements were consistent across all groups.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: The WHOQOL-BREF assessed participants' self-reported QoL in the preceding four weeks and was collected at both timepoints.
items.reasoning: The outcome and its timing (3 and 6 months) are explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: The WHOQOL-BREF has adequate internal consistency and comparable discriminant validity to the original WHOQOL-100
items.reasoning: The authors cite the psychometric validity of the chosen tool.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Assessment and questionnaires were completed at 3 and 6 months after injury for the trauma groups, and questionnaires were completed 3 months apart for the non-injured CC group.
items.reasoning: The measurement protocol was consistent across groups.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the study adjusted for age, gender, and education in the regression, and used comparison groups to control for the general effects of trauma, the sample size for the mTBI group (n=40) is relatively small for a multivariable model, potentially limiting the ability to account for all confounders.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: The first step was to enter age, education, and gender... Only variables that significantly contributed to the variance were kept in the model.
items.reasoning: Key demographics were measured, but specific post-injury treatments or rehabilitation received were not explicitly included as confounders.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1. Demographic and injury information
items.reasoning: Confounders like age and education are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: using accessible medical records.
items.reasoning: Demographic and injury data were sourced from medical records, which is generally reliable.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The three groups (i.e., mTBI, TC and CC) did not significantly differ on gender, age, years of education, or number of comorbidities
items.reasoning: Baseline confounders were assessed identically across groups.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: conducted multiple imputation analysis that used proxies... to predict and replace the missing data on both the independent and dependent variables
items.reasoning: Imputation was applied to both predictors and outcomes.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: A non-injured age-matched comparison group of community-dwelling older adults... was also recruited
items.reasoning: The use of an age-matched community group and a trauma comparison group is a strong design choice to control for age and general injury effects.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: The first step was to enter age, education, and gender using stepwise regression to control for these potentially confounding factors.
items.reasoning: Statistical adjustment was performed via hierarchical regression.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical approach (Linear Mixed Modeling and Hierarchical Regression) is appropriate for longitudinal data. The authors report both significant and non-significant findings transparently.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: We used linear mixed modeling (LMM) to examine differences between groups across the two time-points... Next, we conducted hierarchical regressions
items.reasoning: The analytical plan is detailed and matches the study aims.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: The first step was to enter age, education, and gender... At step 2, 3-month psychological health, GCS... were added
items.reasoning: The hierarchical approach allows for testing the unique contribution of injury factors after controlling for demographics and early psychological health.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: LMM was chosen as the preferred statistical analysis because LMM can account for correlations between repeated measurements
items.reasoning: LMM is the standard for longitudinal data with potential missingness.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: injury variables and 3-month neuropsychological performance did not uniquely contribute to the model
items.reasoning: The authors report non-significant predictors and provide full regression tables (including supplementary references).
